item.title: A strong profit report from SpaceX helps lift tech stocks and Wall Street
item.description: U.S. stocks climbed following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: The U.S. stock market rose Wednesday following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies. The S&P 500 added 0.6 per cent and pulled within 0.8 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 360 points, or 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1 per cent. SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 7.8 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla rose 3.4 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 2.5 per cent, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 10.7 per cent. Expectations are high for profit growth for all kinds of companies during the summer, and they need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. On the losing side of Wall Street was Netflix, which fell 5.3 per cent even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT&T fell 6.4 per cent even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled. After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. Its stock bounced between an early gain of nearly 4 per cent and a drop of 4.5 per cent Wednesday morning before finishing with a dip of 0.5 per cent. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 5 per cent and a drop of more than 6 per cent. Other AI-linked stocks were more resilient, and Nvidia’s rise of 2.5 per cent was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 9.5 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 44.60 points to 7,757.17. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 360.21 to 52,856.09, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 278.04 to 26,702.86. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury erased an early dip and climbed back to 5.12 per cent, where it was late Tuesday. It swung with oil prices, which remained unsteady. The price for a barrel of Brent crude drifted between US$108 and US$111 before settling at US$108.82. It’s been yo-yoing between US$97 and US$112 through October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Michelle Chapman and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

item.title: National Bank looks to modernize personal banking unit to better compete, CEO says
item.description: National Bank’s chief executive says competition is rising in the personal banking space and the lender will look to modernize its operations to attract clients.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — National Bank’s chief executive says competition is rising in the personal banking space and the lender will look to modernize its operations to attract more clients. While speaking at the Canadian Club Toronto on Wednesday, Laurent Ferreira noted that consumer habits are shifting and newer lenders are offering fully digital services that are gaining momentum. Ferreira says the rapid growth of AI will also shift the landscape for deposits and payments. He says the bank views these developments as structural changes with opportunities to gain market share, but that its personal banking segment will undergo changes over the next few years, like becoming more mobile-centric, digital and simple. Ferreira says its strategy may also involve partnering with some of the new players that have better technology or a different business model. As the bank looks to build out its digital platforms, he says it is also increasing investments to protect client data, as AI is being used as a cyber weapon by fraudsters and hostile foreign governments. --- Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

item.title: BMO is ‘leaning into’ the defence industry
item.description: BMO is expanding its focus on defence as the government looks to spend more in the sector as part of its broader build Canada agenda.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: BMO is expanding its focus on defence as the government looks to spend more in the sector as part of its broader build Canada agenda. Darryl White, BMO Financial Group CEO, said that the lender is “responding to the signal” from Canada’s federal government amid commitments to raise defence spending. White said the bank has a long history of operating in the defence industry while serving small and large domestic firms. “We’re taking a strength of ours (and) leaning into it even more heavily than we were before,” he said. BMO said in a news release Wednesday that it will co-host a defence forum in Toronto with the Institute of International Finance on Thursday. The bank said it will involve bringing finance leaders from the Canadian defence industry to discuss opportunities and challenges. The announcement marks another step in BMO honing in on defence. In September, BMO announced plans to mobilize up to $70 billion in new capital over 10 years for key sectors of Canada’s economy, including defence. Other sectors included infrastructure for electricity, energy and transportation as well as oil and gas, mining and AI. Other large banks have made similar moves. CIBC has committed $2 billion to support small and medium-sized defence businesses with dual uses in the civilian sector. Meanwhile, TD Bank committed $150 billion over five years to accelerate investment in key industries including defence. In February, BMO announced it had joined the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB). The bank, spearheaded by NATO countries, is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength. All of Canada’s Big Six banks have put their support behind the DSRB. In an October report, BMO economists forecast that Canada’s pledge to spend five per cent of annual GDP on defence by 2035 would generate about $150 billion in annual economic impact by that year. “We haven’t seen something that can singularly deliver that much economic impact in this country in a very long time,” White said, adding that he is optimistic it can be achieved. “Do I think that the probability of getting there is high? Yes, I do because if you look on whether it’s the procurement side of things or the infrastructure side of things, there are commitments that I believe will be kept and we expect to play a very big part of that.” BMO’s moves come after hundreds of executives and global asset managers assembled in Toronto in September for Canada’s first national investment summit. Prime Minister Mark Carney had set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in new investment to Canada over the next five years. White said that foreign investment sentiment in Canada has changed. “I’ve been watching this for a very long time … over the course of the last couple of years international investors have gotten themselves closer and closer to getting on the field for participation in Canadian investment,” he said. “The summit, I think was a was a nexus where we could bring people as close to the field as you can get.” However, he said summits are generally not where deals get done. “There’s a little bit of romanticizing that goes on around people have summits and cut deals. That’s not really the way it works,” he said. White said it’s a place where people develop more relationships, get themselves closer to the interest in investing, but deals come when the conditions are right and the term sheets start to flow. “I don’t think we’re there yet, but we’ve certainly done a good job laying more groundwork than we have otherwise.” Another sign that BMO is increasing its footprint in the industry was the appointment of Michael Bonner as the enterprise chair of its Canadian defence sector segment. Bonner will also act as a liaison to government agencies and industry associations regarding defence-related financing, export credit, and procurement. “BMO has the experience, expertise and relationships to help clients of all sizes capitalize on that growth,” Bonner said in a news release. White’s comments come as he is scheduled to speak at the Toronto Global Forum on Wednesday. “It brings together leaders from around the world that are shaping their economies and an ability therefore to share best practices against the geopolitical realignment that we’ve got,” he said. Some of the major themes are AI, energy, infrastructure, finance and defence. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026. Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

item.title: ‘We’re going to take care of Bombardier’: Trump backs down on threat against Canadian jet maker
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take “good care” of the company’s workers in Kansas.
item.dc:creator: Graham Richardson
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA – U.S. President Donald Trump appears to be backing away from his threat to shut Canadian aerospace giant Bombardier out of the U.S. market, after learning about the company’s significant operations in Kansas. In September, Trump threatened to block sales of Bombardier jets in the United States amid a growing trade dispute with Canada. “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 7. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’” But while visiting Kansas on Monday, Trump struck a dramatically different tone after learning about Bombardier’s operations in Wichita, where the company employs about 1,500 people. “We’re going to take care of Bombardier,” Trump told 12 News in Kansas. He repeated the sentiment on stage at a rally later in the day. “I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away … I’ll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company,” Trump said. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So, we’ll take care of those people and the jobs.” Dominic LeBlanc, the federal minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, has argued for months that Bombardier is deeply embedded in the American economy. “Bombardier has many hundreds and thousands of employees in the United States and has had for a long time. I had seen a number of legislators in the United States, including Republicans, express concerns this summer when President Trump had made those comments about Bombardier,” said Leblanc. Trump was in Kansas to campaign for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is locked in an unusually competitive re-election fight against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Kansas has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, but polls have shown a close race this year. Trump’s September threat against Bombardier had become a political issue in Kansas because of the company’s 1,500 jobs in Wichita. Marshall was among the Kansas lawmakers who contacted the White House after Trump threatened to block Bombardier from the U.S. market. Trump specifically cited Marshall’s involvement when he told local television Monday that his administration would “take care of Bombardier.” Bombardier employs about 3,500 people across the United States, with more than 40 per cent of those jobs in Wichita. The company last week announced a US$50-million investment in Wichita, home to its U.S. and defence headquarters. “We’re going to find a deal with the United States at some point that’s in the interest of the entire Canadian economy,” said Leblanc.
